research_question: In women with urinary incontinence, what is the effect of indirect training (non-pelvic-floor exercises such as general core, abdominal, hip adductor, or trunk/postural exercises) combined with direct pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT), compared with direct PFMT alone, on incontinence-related quality of life?
treatment_label: Indirect training (core/hip/trunk exercise) combined with direct PFMT
outcome_description: Incontinence-related quality of life measured with condition-specific instruments (e.g. ICIQ-UI SF quality-of-life items/total, King's Health Questionnaire, Incontinence Impact Questionnaire IIQ-7, I-QOL, ICIQ-LUTSqol, Urogenital Distress Inventory impact scores) at post-intervention assessment. Scales where a higher score indicates greater symptom impact/worse quality of life are treated as the reference direction; better-is-higher scales (e.g. I-QOL) are reverse-signed so that a positive effect always favours the combined-training arm.
positive_direction: A positive Hedges g / SMD means that adding indirect training (core, hip, or trunk exercise) to direct PFMT produced BETTER incontinence-related quality of life than direct PFMT alone.
search_queries: pelvic floor muscle training plus core stability exercise urinary incontinence women randomized trial quality of life
hip adductor abdominal trunk exercise added to pelvic floor muscle training female urinary incontinence controlled trial
adjunct core strengthening pelvic floor muscle training incontinence quality of life ICIQ King's Health Questionnaire effect
inclusion_criteria: Adult women with any type of urinary incontinence (stress, urgency, or mixed), including postpartum and postmenopausal samples

Compares a treatment arm receiving indirect/non-pelvic-floor exercise (core, abdominal, hip, trunk, postural, or general exercise) TOGETHER WITH direct pelvic floor muscle training against a control arm receiving direct pelvic floor muscle training alone
Reports some quantitative incontinence-related quality-of-life outcome (means and SDs, change scores, t/F statistics, or other data from which an effect size can be derived)
exclusion_criteria: Not an original empirical study (systematic review, meta-analysis, editorial, opinion piece, protocol, conference abstract without data, or purely theoretical/narrative paper)
No comparison between a treatment and a control condition (single-arm, pre-post only, or no direct-PFMT-alone comparator)
No quantitative outcome data usable for an effect size (no means+SDs, t/F values, proportions, or odds ratios reported or derivable)

Wrong comparison or topic: indirect training ALONE versus PFMT (no PFMT in treatment arm), co-ordinated training in which body movements are performed with simultaneous pelvic floor muscle contraction versus PFMT, comparisons where the control arm is not direct PFMT alone, non-exercise adjuncts only (electrical stimulation, biofeedback, pessary, drugs, surgery), male or paediatric samples, faecal incontinence or pelvic organ prolapse only, or otherwise unrelated to the research topic
moderators_to_extract: Type of indirect training (core/abdominal, hip adductor, trunk/postural, general fitness)
Type of urinary incontinence (stress, urgency, mixed)
Population subgroup (postpartum, postmenopausal, general adult women)
Intervention duration in weeks and supervision level (supervised vs home-based)
Quality-of-life instrument used (ICIQ-UI SF, KHQ, IIQ-7, I-QOL, other)
Sample size category and risk-of-bias / randomisation quality
effect_size_note: Pool as standardised mean difference (Hedges-corrected) because quality of life is measured on heterogeneous condition-specific instruments. Scale direction must be harmonised before pooling: impact/severity scales (ICIQ-UI SF, KHQ, IIQ-7, UDI) have higher = worse and are signed so improvement is positive; I-QOL and similar better-is-higher scales are reverse-coded. Use post-intervention means and SDs where available, otherwise change-from-baseline means with SDs, and prefer the longest post-treatment assessment within the intervention period when multiple are reported (all timepoints pooled into one estimate).
